title: Analyzing Code Line-by-Line
summary: A mechanical technique for turning any function into a Big-O: sequential statements add, nested loops multiply, conditionals take the worst branch, and called functions bring their own cost along.

slides.markdown:
You already know what O(n) and O(n²) mean. The skill interviewers actually test is different: can you look at **unfamiliar source code** and derive its complexity on the spot, out loud, in under a minute?

That derivation is mechanical, not intuitive, once you know four rules:

1. Sequential statements **add**.
2. Nested loops **multiply**.
3. Conditionals take the **worst-case branch**.
4. A called function's complexity gets **multiplied in**, not treated as free.

Miss any one of these and you'll misjudge real code — usually by treating a hidden O(n) call as O(1), which is the single most common Big-O mistake candidates make once problems stop being toy loops.

slides.subTitle: The slowest one dominates
slides.markdown:
If a function runs one block, then another, their costs **add**: a function that does an O(n) pass followed by an O(n²) pass is O(n) + O(n²).

Big-O then drops the lower-order term, exactly like it drops constants: O(n) + O(n²) simplifies to **O(n²)**, because the quadratic term swamps the linear one for large n.

The general rule: when you have a sequence of blocks, **the slowest block is the answer** — you almost never need to write out the sum. Three O(n) passes back to back is still just O(n), not O(3n); one O(n²) block after ten O(n) blocks is still O(n²).

This is why "how many passes does your solution make?" is a weaker interview question than it sounds — three passes over the array is the same complexity as one.

slides.subTitle: Why two nested O(n) loops become O(n²)
slides.markdown:
A loop that runs n times, with an inner loop that also runs n times **for every outer iteration**, does n × n = n² total iterations. That's the entire reason nested loops are the classic quadratic shape.

The multiplication rule generalizes past equal bounds: an outer loop of size **n** wrapping an inner loop of size **m** is **O(n·m)**, not O(n²) — collapsing two independent sizes into one variable is a common analysis error (see naming your variables, `what-big-o-actually-claims`).

Depth matters too: three loops nested inside each other, each running n times, multiply to **O(n³)**. The rule is purely structural — it doesn't matter what the loop body does, as long as the body itself is O(1); if the body does real work, that cost multiplies in as well (Rule 4).

slides.sectionTitle: Rule 3: conditionals take the worst branch
Walking a real function line by line
slides.markdown:
```python
def count_pairs(arr, k):
    n = len(arr)
    seen = set()             # O(1)
    count = 0
    for i in range(n):       # runs n times
        if arr[i] in seen:   # O(1) average — set membership
            count += 1
        seen.add(arr[i] - k) # O(1) average
        seen.add(arr[i] + k) # O(1) average
    return count              # O(1)
```

Line by line: the setup is O(1). The loop runs n times (Rule 2's single-loop case: n × O(1)). Inside, every statement is O(1) average — one membership check, two inserts — so the loop body doesn't add a hidden multiplier.

Total: **O(n)** average time, O(n) space for the set. Notice there's no nested loop here at all — the shape *looks* like it could hide an O(n²), but every line inside is genuinely constant, so it collapses to linear. Reading each line's true cost, not just counting loops, is what separates real analysis from pattern-matching on indentation.

slides.sectionTitle: Rule 4: a called function brings its cost with it
slides.markdown:
A function call inside a loop isn't free just because it's one line. Its own complexity **multiplies into** the loop's, exactly like a nested loop would.

```python
for x in arr:            # n iterations
    if x in some_list:    # O(len(some_list)) per call!
        ...
```

If `some_list` has m elements, this is **O(n·m)**, not O(n) — the membership check is a hidden inner loop wearing a function-call disguise. The same applies to calling `sorted()` inside a loop (O(n log n) per call, so O(n² log n) total), or calling a recursive helper whose own complexity is O(log n) (making the outer loop O(n log n)).

The habit to build: before you call any line O(1), ask **what does that call actually do underneath**, not what it looks like from the call site.

slides.subTitle: `list.pop(0)` isn't O(1)
slides.markdown:
`list.pop()` — removing the **last** element — is O(1): no other element moves. `list.pop(0)` — removing the **first** element — is **O(n)**: every remaining element has to shift left by one to keep the array contiguous (the same shifting cost covered in `arrays-strings`).

The two calls look identical in complexity from the call site — one line, one argument — but their cost differs by a full order. A loop that calls `pop(0)` n times is quietly **O(n²)**, not O(n), and this exact bug is common enough in interview code that it's worth naming out loud: "I'm popping from the front here, which is O(n) per call, so this loop is O(n²) — let me use a deque instead," is a stronger answer than writing the buggy version and hoping no one asks.

The general lesson: know the underlying data structure well enough that "it's one method call" stops being a proxy for "it's cheap."

slides.subTitle: `x in list` vs `x in set`
slides.markdown:
The same-looking `in` check hides two very different costs depending on the container:

| Check | Underlying cost | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `x in list` | O(n) | scans elements one by one until a match or the end |
| `x in set` / `x in dict` | O(1) average | hashes `x` and probes one bucket (see `hash-table-mechanics`) |

A loop with `x in list` inside it is **O(n²)**; swap that list for a set and the same loop drops to **O(n)** — no algorithmic redesign, just a container swap. This is the single highest-leverage micro-optimization in interview coding: whenever you write "check if I've seen this before," reach for a set by default, and only use a list if you specifically need order or duplicates preserved.

The cost is genuinely invisible at the call site — `in` reads identically either way — which is exactly why this table matters more than it looks like it should.

slides.sectionTitle: A loop bounded by a shrinking variable
slides.subTitle: Not by the input size
slides.markdown:
Not every loop's iteration count is n. Some loops are bounded by a variable that shrinks or grows independently of the input size, and reading the loop header as "it runs n times" without checking is a common miscount.

```python
def count_digits(x):
    count = 0
    while x > 0:
        x //= 10      # x shrinks by a factor of 10 each time
        count += 1
    return count
```

This loop's bound is **the number of digits in x**, not x itself — it runs O(log₁₀ x) times, because dividing by 10 repeatedly is exactly the halving-style shrink that produces a logarithm (see `the-growth-rate-ladder`). Treating it as "a while loop over x" and guessing O(x) overstates the true cost by an exponential factor.

The fix is always the same: identify what actually changes each iteration and how fast, then derive the count from that — don't pattern-match on "loop" meaning "linear in the input."

A staff-level walkthrough of unfamiliar code says, out loud, in order:

1. **Is this sequential or nested?** Sequential adds and keeps the max; nested multiplies.
2. **Does it branch?** Take the worst-case branch's cost, and say you're doing so.
3. **Does any line call another function, method, or built-in?** Look up or state its real cost — don't assume O(1) from syntax alone.
4. **Is any loop's bound a transformed variable** (digit count, shrinking range, recursion depth) rather than the raw input size?

Run those four checks over any function and you'll rarely be wrong, and you'll rarely need to trace execution by hand. The rest of this group extends the same discipline to two shapes plain line-counting can't handle on its own: recursive calls, which need a recurrence relation instead of a loop count, and amortized costs, where one expensive operation is deliberately spread across many cheap ones.
